head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Binary search on a property (up or down) rather than on a value
Still climbing: the peak lies to the right
Falling, or at the peak: the peak is at mid or to its left, so keep mid

blocks.h: Why is binary search valid on a mountain?
p: A mountain rises strictly then falls strictly, so the slope test is monotone: 'rising' holds everywhere left of the peak and 'falling' everywhere from the peak on. That is a sorted True/False pattern, and binary search finds its boundary.

852.takeaway: Binary search on the slope: rising means the peak is right of mid, otherwise at mid or left.

p: `n = 10`: four seatings, one leave, one seating:

blocks.h: Why compare the right edge after the loop?
p: The right edge is a different kind of gap: sitting at seat n−1 gives the full distance to the last student, not half. The edge distance is compared to `best` once with `>`, so ties still go to the earlier seat.

What it does
Reach for it when

A mask with all key bits set: the goal
BFS (Breadth-First Search) state is the cell AND the keys held; the same cell with different keys is a different state
Extending BFS state with extra information
Picking up a key sets its bit
Tests whether the key for this lock (A=0, …) is held; if not the lock blocks the move

p: Grid `["@.a..","###.#","b.A.B"]`. Layers explored (cell row, col, key bits):
bullets: The first state holding all 2 keys appears after 8 steps.

blocks.h: Why must the key set be part of the state?
p: Walking a cell twice is useful when the second visit carries more keys, because it may open doors that were closed the first time. Marking only the cell as visited would block those revisits and give wrong or no answers. With at most 6 keys there are at most 64 key sets per cell, so the state space stays small.

864.takeaway: BFS over (cell, key bitmask): revisits are allowed only when you hold a different set of keys.

867.takeaway: Transpose with zip(*matrix): rows become columns.

p: `[1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8]`: pairs whose sequence reaches length 4 or more (earlier triples of length 3 are not listed):

blocks.h: Why is the pair (j, k) enough as the state?
p: Once the last two numbers are known, the whole sequence is determined backwards: the previous number is their difference. So the best length ending at a pair depends only on the best length ending at the pair before it.

Stops when fast has no two nodes ahead

bullets: When `fast` reaches the last node, `slow` is at the middle (3).

p: For `1→2→3→4` the loop ends with `fast = None` and `slow` on `3`, the second middle, which is what the problem asks for. Changing the condition to `while fast.next and fast.next.next` would return the first middle (2).

bullets: Space: O(1). Counting the length first and walking n/2 steps takes two passes.

876.takeaway: Fast pointer moves twice as fast; when it runs out, slow is at the middle (the second middle for even lengths).

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when

Caching results of a pure function
Left subtree sizes 1, 3, 5, …: a full tree has an odd number of nodes on each side
The right side gets the rest after the root and the left side
Combines every left shape with every right shape
Even n has no full binary tree

p: The number of shapes f(k) for each odd k:

blocks.h: Why are subtrees shared between trees?
p: The cached lists contain the same node objects, so different result trees point to the same subtrees. That is safe because trees are only read (the problem accepts any one-to-one structure), and it saves memory and time. The cost is that mutating one tree would also change others.

bullets: Time and space: proportional to the number of trees generated, which is the Catalan number C((n−1)/2) in the node count, e.g. 5 for n = 7.
Memoization stops the repeated generation of equal sizes.

894.takeaway: Recursive construction with memoization: root + every (left shape × right shape) with odd sizes.

What it does

One die roll: the next 1 to 6 squares
A snake or ladder at the landing square sends you to its destination, but only once (you do not chain)
BFS (Breadth-First Search) visits squares layer by layer, so the first arrival at the end is the minimum number of moves
Shortest path in an unweighted graph

p: 3×3 board with a ladder from square 2 to square 8. Each row expands one queue entry (square, moves taken):
bullets: The end (square 9) is reached after 2 moves.

blocks.h: Why BFS rather than DFS (Depth-First Search)?
p: Every die roll is one move and all moves cost the same, so the shortest path is found by exploring in layers. DFS could find a long path first and would need extra bookkeeping to find the minimum.

bullets: Time: O(n²) squares with up to 6 rolls each.
Space: O(n²) for `seen` and the queue.

909.takeaway: BFS over squares 1..n², with a helper converting the zigzag numbering to board coordinates and following ladders/snakes once.

blocks.h: Why merge sort and not quicksort here?
p: The problem forbids built-in sorting and requires O(n log n); merge sort meets it in the worst case with no randomization.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Kadane's algorithm: the best subarray sum ending here
The same idea for the minimum
A circular subarray is the total minus the minimum non-wrapping subarray left in the middle
If every number is negative, the complement would be an empty subarray (sum 0), which is not allowed, so use the plain maximum

bullets: Options: normal max = 7; wrapping = total − best_min = 7 − -3 = 10. Answer 10 (take 5 and the 5 that wraps around).

p: A circular subarray that wraps around the end leaves a contiguous block unused in the middle. The sum of what you take is the total minus that unused block, and it is largest when the unused block is the minimum subarray.

918.takeaway: Circular maximum subarray = max(Kadane maximum, total − Kadane minimum), except when all numbers are negative.

blocks.h: Why include `row` and the value in the sort key?
p: Within a column, nodes must appear top to bottom, and two nodes in the same row and column must be ordered by value. The tuple `(col, row, value)` provides exactly that order in one sort.
